535	4.3 Inference Speed
536	Each model was run three times per batch size,
537	and wall-clock time was recorded for each run.
538	Our primary metric, output rate, is defined as the
539	number of output tokens divided by adjusted wall
540	time (tokens/s). Output tokens were counted by re-
541	tokenizing the generated hypotheses using the Aya
542	Expanse 8B tokenizer. To isolate model initializa-
543	tion overhead, we performed a separate “warmup”
544	run per model, decoding a single short sentence
545	with batch size 1. The average wall time of warmup
546	runs was subtracted from the total wall time to
547	compute an adjusted speed metric. We also tested
548	multiple batch sizes to analyze throughput scaling.
549	The results for primary systems are presented on
550	Figure 1.
551	As expected, inference speed scales with batch
552	size, but not uniformly. Vicomtech’s systems
553	scaled most efficiently from 70 tokens/s at batch
554	size 1 to nearly 1000 tokens/s at 512. Some mod-
555	els saturated early, showing minimal speedup with
556	larger batch sizes or even failing to produce out-
557	puts.
558	5 Conclusion and Future Directions
559	The final results of the WMT25 shared task on
560	model compression are summarized in Table 4.
561	Figure 2 shows Pareto front comparisons across
562	evaluation criteria.
563	The key findings can be summarized as follows:
564	• BitsAndBytes baselines and LeanAya main-
565	tained translation quality with moderate speed
566	and model size reduction;
567	• Vicomtech’s systems achieved best compres-
568	sion rates, latency and throughput thanks to
569	efficient batch scaling, but at the cost of trans-
570	lation quality;
571	• Quantization has emerged as the most popular
572	approach for its simplicity and effectiveness;
573	• Hallucinations in compressed outputs reveal
574	the fragility of the current approaches and
575	the need for more robust evaluation and
576	compression-aware training techniques.
577	Overall, despite the moderate participation in
578	this shared task limited the breadth of exploration,
579	several submissions showed promising results. The
580	results of this evaluation campaign highlight that
581	task-specific compression of LLMs still warrants
582	===== PAGE 7 =====
583	490
584	more research efforts, especially at high compres-
585	sion rates required for running systems on edge
586	devices. The smallest model still requires almost
587	3GB of disk space, which is incompatible with
588	many edge devices that are equipped with a few
589	hundred MB of memory (Cai et al., 2022). Addi-
590	tionally, high compression rates result in a signifi-
591	cant performance drop. We believe that pushing the
592	boundaries of compression rates and reducing the
593	quality degradation in such settings represent the
594	most interesting challenges for future research on
595	the topic and for participants of the future editions
596	of the task.
597	Looking ahead, future iterations of this task
598	could benefit from expanding the evaluation to
599	more language pairs, aligning more tightly with
600	the evaluation benchmark at the GenMT task, and
601	including human assessments of the outputs.
602	6 Limitations
603	This study offers an early glimpse into the land-
604	scape of model compression for machine transla-
605	tion, but several limitations constrain the gener-
606	ality of its findings. First, the participation was
607	only modest, all systems compressed the same base
608	model (Aya Expanse 8B) and primarily focused on
609	one language pair (Czech→German). Second, the
610	submissions relied mainly on quantization, with
611	limited exploration of other well-established com-
612	pression techniques such as parameter pruning or
613	knowledge distillation. Third, only one system
614	used vLLM infrastructure, limiting comparability.
615	Lastly, quality assessment depended solely on
616	automatic metrics (COMET and MetricX). We did
617	not conduct human evaluation or cross-language
618	validation. We also did not present some important
619	deployment metrics (e.g., memory usage, latency,
620	energy consumption), which narrows the conclu-
621	sions.

Research question: "Define a rigorous, publication-credible EVALUATION PROTOCOL for healing-free low-bit quantization of machine-translation LLMs, and pin down exactly what the WMT25 Model Compression Shared Task requires. With specifics, numbers, and citations:
1. WMT25 Model Compression Shared Task (Gaido et al. 2025, https://aclanthology.org/2025.wmt-1.25/): the EXACT primary + secondary metrics (XCOMET-XL and MetricX-24 — which checkpoints/versions, score scales), the baseline model (Aya Expanse 8B), the language pairs/directions, the on-disk-size and tokens/sec (batch sizes) protocol, the submission rules, and every submitted system with its reported XCOMET-XL/MetricX/size/speed numbers (LeanAya, Vicomtech/GeLaCo+GKD/+Q4, TCD-Kreasof, others). Reconstruct the quality-vs-size Pareto frontier and the explicit gap.
2. METRIC RELIABILITY at low bit-width: evidence that COMET/XCOMET understate quantization damage vs human eval (Marchisio et al. EMNLP 2024, arXiv:2407.03211 — exact deltas); how XCOMET-XL error spans can diagnose WHAT breaks under quantization (mistranslation vs omission vs wrong-script vs hallucination); COMET vs MetricX-24 agreement/disagreement; how COMET behaves on EMPTY/DEGENERATE outputs (does it give spuriously high scores?). chrF++ vs COMET when outputs collapse.
3. RECOMMENDED protocol for our paper: which metrics to report, number of sentences, decoding (greedy vs beam), whether to use each model's chat template vs a generic prompt, baselines to include, statistical tests / confidence intervals, and a low-cost human-eval or stress-test component for 2-3 bit claims.

content.content:
# MetricX-24 Score Scale

Based on the documentation, MetricX-24 uses a score range of **0 to 25, where lower scores indicate better quality** (it predicts an error score).

## Key Quote on Score Direction

The documentation states: "the output from the MetricX-23 models is a score in the range [0, 25] where lower is better (i.e., it predicts an error score)."

This same principle applies to MetricX-24, which uses the same scoring approach. The models are designed to predict translation quality as error measurements rather than quality ratings, meaning:

- **0** = Perfect or near-perfect translation (no errors)
- **25** = Worst possible translation (maximum errors)

The scoring system automatically clips predicted values to stay within this [0, 25] range: "the metric scores get automatically clipped at 0 and 25, to ensure they are strictly in the [0, 25] range."

content.text: The GitHub repo confirms the correct direction: lower is better (error score). The model card fetch's "higher is better" claim was a hallucination by the summarizer. I'll report the verified facts.
